title: The New World in depth
lead: The New World at Advanced depth: the label laws behind every number, the nested appellations, and the regions the Court lists from Missouri to Central Otago.

intro.title: EVERY COUNTRY'S LABEL MATH
intro.text: Advanced questions turn on the law. Learn each country's minimum for a place name, then the stricter extras.

tiers.name: U.S. federal

tiers.name: South Africa

sections.name: U.S. law: AVAs and the TTB label
sections.source: eCFR 27 CFR parts 4 and 9; TTB established-AVA lists

lines.label: The AVA
lines.text: A grape-growing area with features that set it apart, a name and a mapped boundary, approved by TTB. There are 280; California has 154.

lines.label: Label math
lines.text: From Level 2: 75% grape, 85% AVA, 95% vintage with an AVA. Advanced adds the state, county, multi-county and multi-state rules.

know: An AVA petition must prove the name, the boundary and the distinguishing features: climate, geology, soils, physical features and elevation.
A state or county name needs 75% of the fruit; two or three counties, or two or three contiguous states, need 100%, with each share on the label.
An AVA wine must be fully finished in the state (or one of the states) where the AVA lies.
Estate bottled: the winery sits in the AVA, grows every grape on land it owns or controls (a lease of 3+ years) and never lets the wine leave.
Burgundy, Chablis, Champagne, Port and Sherry are semi-generic names in U.S. law: usable only with the true origin shown.

sections.name: California, Oregon and Washington
sections.source: TTB AVA lists; California Business and Professions Code 25240; Wine Institute; Oregon Administrative Rules 845-010; Oregon Wine Board; Washington State Wine Commission

lines.label: California
lines.text: On average 81% of U.S. wine, and 154 AVAs. Since January 1, 1990, a Napa sub-AVA label must also say 'Napa Valley'.

lines.label: Oregon and Washington
lines.text: Oregon goes past federal law: 90% for most grape names, 95% for a place, 100% Oregon fruit. Washington grows in the dry, irrigated Columbia Valley.

know: Eleven Paso Robles district AVAs, such as Adelaida District and Templeton Gap District, were all established on October 9, 2014.
Oregon allows 75% for 18 listed grapes, including Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Tempranillo and Zinfandel. Pinot Noir is not on the list.
Since 2023, an Oregon label naming a nested Willamette Valley AVA must also say 'Willamette Valley'.
Oregon bans semi-generic names such as 'Chablis'; 'Claret' survives only for 100% Bordeaux-grape brands approved in 2004-2006.
Washington: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Riesling and Syrah are over 80% of production; the Columbia Valley gets 6-8 inches of rain.

items.label: FEDERAL
items.title: The floor
items.text:
Grape name: 75%

Semi-generic names allowed with true origin

items.label: OREGON

AVA or county: 95%, all fruit Oregon

Semi-generic names banned

sections.name: New York, other states, Canada and Mexico
sections.source: TTB AVA lists; Missouri Secretary of State; Wines of Canada; VQA Ontario; Court of Master Sommeliers curriculum guide (Mexico)

lines.label: New York and beyond
lines.text: Finger Lakes (1982) holds Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake; Long Island (2001) holds The Hamptons and North Fork. The first AVA of all was Augusta, Missouri, in 1980.

lines.label: Canada and Mexico
lines.text: VQA runs Ontario and British Columbia. Mexico, the oldest wine industry outside Europe, has no appellation law, per the Court; Valle de Guadalupe is the focus.

know: Augusta, Missouri became the first AVA on June 20, 1980, seven months ahead of Napa Valley.
Norton (Cynthiana), a Vitis aestivalis grape, is Missouri's state grape and North America's oldest variety still grown commercially.
Other states' AVAs: Monticello (VA), Texas High Plains and Texas Hill Country, Snake River Valley (ID, OR), Old Mission and Leelanau Peninsulas (MI).
VQA Icewine: frozen on the vine, picked below -8 °C, juice of 35° Brix or more. Hybrids are barred from Icewine except Vidal.
Spanish law banned winemaking in New Spain from 1595 until Mexico's independence in 1821.

sections.name: Argentina, Chile and Uruguay
sections.source: Chile Decree 464 (SAG); Wines of Chile; Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura (Argentina); Uruguay harvest statistics as reported by Montevideo Portal

lines.label: Chile
lines.text: Decree 464 maps six regions from Atacama to Austral, then subregions, zones and areas. A DO, grape or vintage needs 75%; Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes needs 85%.

lines.label: Argentina and Uruguay
lines.text: Argentina has three tiers: IP (80%, table wine), IG and DOC. Uruguay's signature is Tannat: 1,610 of 5,991 ha in 2020, mostly in Canelones.

know: Chile's six regions, north to south: Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur and Austral.
Secano Interior is Chile's special DO for País and Cinsault from dry-farmed areas such as Cauquenes, Chillán and Coelemu.
Argentina has only two DOCs, both in Mendoza: Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael. An INV report counted 110 IGs.
Cuyo IG covers Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis; Valle de Uco IG covers San Carlos, Tunuyán and Tupungato.
Only 'Valle de Cafayate' may go on a label, because 'Cafayate' alone is a registered trademark.

rows.name: DOC
rows.note: Only two: Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael

rows.name: IG
rows.note: Quality wines; Valle de Uco is the most used

rows.name: IP
rows.note: Table and regional wines, 80% from the place

sections.name: Australia and New Zealand
sections.source: Wine Australia (GI register, blending rules, Label Integrity Program); New Zealand Winegrowers

lines.label: Australia
lines.text: GIs run zone, region, subregion; South Eastern Australia is a zone spanning all of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania. The Label Integrity Program makes every seller keep records that back the label.

lines.label: New Zealand
lines.text: Vineyards stretch 1,600 km, none more than 130 km from the sea. Marlborough holds about two-thirds of the vines; Hawke's Bay is second.

know: An Australian blend may name up to three GIs, each over 5% of the wine, in descending order.
Grapes picked from September 1 to December 31 count as the next year's vintage in Australia.
'Barossa style' or 'Champagne method' is banned on Australian labels, even with the true origin shown.
Central Otago subregions: Gibbston (highest), Bannockburn (warm, dry, earliest), Cromwell/Lowburn/Pisa, Bendigo, Wanaka, Alexandra.
Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand began in 1995 and covers 98% of vineyard area.

sections.name: South Africa
sections.source: Wines of South Africa (Wine of Origin scheme; winegrowing areas); Court of Master Sommeliers, Advanced Theory Exam guide

lines.label: Wine of Origin
lines.text: Origin control became law in 1973, and a WO place name means 100% of the grapes come from there. Units nest from geographical unit down to a single vineyard.

lines.label: The six units
lines.text: Western Cape, Northern Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Free State. The Western Cape holds five regions: Breede River Valley, Cape South Coast, Coastal Region, Klein Karoo, Olifants River.

know: A district is larger and less uniform than a ward but still has a distinctive climate; the Court names 'districts vs wards' as a topic.
Some wards, such as Cederberg and Bamboes Bay, sit outside any district.
Cape Coastal is an overarching region joining the Coastal Region and the Cape South Coast, so maritime wines can be blended under one name.
Estate wine is grown, made and bottled on one unit; a single vineyard may not exceed 6 hectares.
WOSA counts 32 districts and about 102 wards across some 86,525 ha of wine grapes.

mixups.why: Augusta, Missouri was the first AVA (1980). Napa Valley was the second (1981).
Cuyo IG covers three provinces. Luján de Cuyo is one of Argentina's only two DOCs, inside Mendoza.
Cape Coastal is an overarching region that contains the Coastal Region and the Cape South Coast.
Both are Central Otago. Gibbston is high and late; Bannockburn is warm, dry and early.

facts.fact: 27 CFR 4.25(e)(1): an American viticultural area is a delimited grape-growing region with distinguishing features, a name and a delineated boundary established under part 9.

27 CFR 4.25(e)(3): a viticultural area appellation needs at least 85 percent of the wine from grapes grown in the area, and American wine must be fully finished in the State (or one of the States) where the AVA lies.
27 CFR 4.25(e)(4): overlapping viticultural areas may be used together if at least 85 percent of the wine comes from the overlapping area.

27 CFR 4.25(b)(1): a country, State or county appellation for American wine needs at least 75 percent of the wine from fruit grown there; a State appellation must be fully finished in that State or an adjacent State; a county appellation in that county's State.

27 CFR 4.25(c)-(d): two or three counties in one State, or two or three contiguous States, may be named only if all of the fruit was grown there and the percentage from each is shown on the label (plus or minus 2 percent).
27 CFR 4.23(c)(1): a Vitis labrusca variety may be named at 51 percent, with the statement 'contains not less than 51 percent (variety)' unless 75 percent or more is that variety.
27 CFR 4.23(d): two or more varieties may be named only if all the grapes are of those varieties and each percentage is shown (plus or minus 2 percent).

27 CFR 4.26: Estate bottled requires a viticultural area appellation; the winery must be in the AVA, grow all grapes on land it owns or controls in the AVA, and crush, ferment, finish, age and bottle in a continuous process on its premises; 'controlled' means a lease or similar agreement of at least 3 years; no other term may indicate combined growing and bottling.
27 CFR 4.27(a): vintage wine with a viticultural area appellation needs at least 95 percent from the labeled year; with another appellation, 85 percent.

27 CFR 4.24(b)(2): semi-generic names include Burgundy, Claret, Chablis, Champagne, Chianti, Madeira, Marsala, Port, Sherry and Tokay; they may be used only with an appellation disclosing the true origin. 4.24(c)(2): Napa Valley and Lake Erie are examples of nongeneric names.
27 CFR 4.36(b)(1): the alcohol tolerance is 1 percent for wine over 14 percent ABV and 1.5 percent for wine at 14 percent or less.
27 CFR 4.21(a)(5)-(6): table wine is not over 14 percent alcohol; dessert wine is over 14 and not over 24 percent.
27 CFR 9.11: any person may petition TTB to establish an AVA, or change an AVA's boundary or name.

27 CFR 9.12(a): an AVA petition must include name evidence (from sources independent of the petitioner), boundary evidence, distinguishing features (climate, geology, soils, physical features, elevation) and USGS maps with a boundary description.
TTB: 'Currently, there are 280 established AVAs in the United States.' California has the most AVAs, with 154.
TTB establishment dates: Augusta (MO) 6/20/1980 is the first AVA; Napa Valley 1/28/1981; Santa Maria Valley 8/5/1981.
Wine Institute: California produces an average of 81 percent of total U.S. wine production.

California Business and Professions Code 25240: wine labeled with an AVA (other than Napa Valley) located entirely within a county of the 29th class must bear 'Napa Valley' in direct conjunction; applies to all wines bottled on or after January 1, 1990; not required when the AVA name already includes 'Napa Valley'.

TTB dates: eleven San Luis Obispo County AVAs, including Adelaida District, Creston District, El Pomar District, Paso Robles Estrella District, Paso Robles Geneseo District, Paso Robles Highlands District, Paso Robles Willow Creek District, San Juan Creek, San Miguel District, Santa Margarita Ranch and Templeton Gap District, were established 10/9/2014.

TTB AVA table: Adelaida District lies within the Central Coast and Paso Robles AVAs; Rutherford (Napa County) lies within the Napa Valley and North Coast AVAs; Dundee Hills (Yamhill County) lies within the Willamette Valley AVA.
TTB dates: Sta. Rita Hills 5/31/2001; Crystal Springs of Napa Valley 10/16/2024.

OAR 845-010-0915: a single grape variety name requires at least 90 percent of that variety; 18 listed varieties need 75 percent: Cabernet franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Durif (Petite Sirah), Grenache, Malbec, Marsanne, Merlot, Mourvèdre, Petit Verdot, Roussanne, Sangiovese, Sauvignon blanc, Sémillon, Syrah, Tannat, Tempranillo, Zinfandel.
OAR 845-010-0920: if the label names Oregon, an Oregon county, or an AVA wholly in Oregon, all grapes must be grown in Oregon and 95 percent within the named appellation.
OAR 845-010-0923: from January 1, 2023, a label naming a nested AVA wholly or partly within the Willamette Valley AVA must carry the phrase 'Willamette Valley' on the brand label.

OAR 845-010-0930: semi-generic names may not be used as a class or type on an Oregon wine label; 'Claret' is allowed only for 100 percent Bordeaux-variety blends whose federal label approval was issued between December 1, 2004 and March 10, 2006.

Oregon Wine Board: Oregon is home to 23 AVAs; eleven are nested inside the Willamette Valley AVA (Chehalem Mountains, Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, Laurelwood District, Lower Long Tom, McMinnville, Mount Pisgah Polk County, Ribbon Ridge, Tualatin Hills, Van Duzer Corridor, Yamhill-Carlton).

Washington State Wine Commission (stats as of August 2026): Washington is the 2nd largest wine-producing state, with 22 AVAs, 35,000 acres of wine grapes and 6-8 inches of annual rainfall in the Columbia Valley.

Washington State Wine Commission: the Columbia Valley sits in the rain shadow of the Olympics and Cascades, so irrigation is required in most places; Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Riesling and Syrah make up over 80 percent of production.

Washington State Wine Commission: Columbia Valley soils are wind-blown loess over Missoula Flood deposits and slackwater sediments, on basalt bedrock; Yakima Fold Belt anticlines give south-facing slopes (Rattlesnake Hills, Red Mountain, Candy Mountain, Royal Slope, Horse Heaven Hills, Columbia Gorge).

TTB dates: Finger Lakes 9/1/1982; Cayuga Lake 3/25/1988; Seneca Lake 7/3/2003; The Hamptons, Long Island 5/16/1985; North Fork of Long Island 10/10/1986; Long Island 5/15/2001; Lake Erie (NY, OH, PA) 10/21/1983; Hudson River Region 6/4/1982; Niagara Escarpment 9/8/2005; Upper Hudson 12/6/2018.
TTB AVA table: Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake lie within the Finger Lakes AVA; North Fork of Long Island and The Hamptons, Long Island lie within the Long Island AVA.

TTB dates: Monticello (VA) 1/23/1984; Texas Hill Country 11/29/1991; Texas High Plains 3/2/1993; Snake River Valley (ID, OR) 3/9/2007; Old Mission Peninsula (MI) 6/8/1987; Leelanau Peninsula (MI) 3/30/1982; Middle Rio Grande Valley (NM) 2/2/1988; Hermann (MO) 8/18/1983.

Missouri Secretary of State: the Norton/Cynthiana grape, designated Vitis aestivalis, became Missouri's official state grape in 2003; it is called North America's oldest grape variety commercially grown today.

Wines of Canada: primary regions are the Niagara Peninsula (Ontario) and the Okanagan Valley (British Columbia), with smaller areas in Québec and Nova Scotia; Ontario produces over 90 percent of Canada's Icewine, made primarily from Vidal, Riesling and Cabernet Franc.

Wines of Canada: Ontario appellations are Niagara Peninsula (+10 sub-appellations), Prince Edward County and Lake Erie North Shore (+1); BC lists Okanagan Valley (+4 sub-appellations), Similkameen Valley, Vancouver Island and others; VQA operates in Ontario and British Columbia.

Wines of Canada: Québec uses cold-hardy hybrids such as Frontenac Noir, Blanc and Gris, Vidal, Seyval Blanc and Marquette; Nova Scotia grows mainly hybrids (L'Acadie, Seyval Blanc, Marechal Foch and others) and is known for sparkling wine and aromatic white Tidal Bay.

VQA Ontario: VQA is 100% Ontario; most declarations need 85 percent (vintage 85 percent); 'VQA Niagara Peninsula' means at least 85 percent Niagara grapes, while a sub-appellation such as Four Mile Creek means 100 percent from there.

VQA Ontario: Icewine grapes freeze naturally on the vine, are harvested below -8 °C and yield juice of at least 35° Brix; Special Select Late Harvest needs 30° Brix, Select Late Harvest 26°, Late Harvest 22°.
VQA Ontario: wines with hybrid content may use only the Ontario appellation and cannot use terms such as estate bottled, vineyard designation, Traditional Method or Icewine, except Vidal Icewine.

Court curriculum guide (Mexico): Mexico is the oldest wine industry outside Europe; from 1595 winemaking in New Spain was prohibited by Spanish law until independence in 1821; the modern industry dates from the 1970s.

Court curriculum guide (Mexico, Certified column): 'No laws!'; Baja California's Valle de Guadalupe has a Mediterranean climate, with southwest-to-northeast valleys bringing Pacific fog and cooling breezes; sandy soils; irrigation essential; Italian, French and Spanish grapes in non-traditional blends.

Chile Decree 464: wine regions are Atacama (Copiapó, Huasco), Coquimbo (Elqui, Limarí, Choapa), Aconcagua (Aconcagua, Casablanca, San Antonio valleys and others), Valle Central (Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule), Sur (Itata, Bío Bío, Malleco) and Austral (Cautín, Osorno).
Chile Decree 464 Art. 3-5: a DO on the label needs at least 75 percent of the wine from that place; a named variety at least 75 percent; a vintage at least 75 percent.

Chile Decree 464 Art. 5 bis: labels may add 'Andes', 'Entre Cordilleras' or 'Costa' (Andes, the intermediate depression, the Pacific) if at least 85 percent of the wine comes from areas declared as that type.
Chile Decree 464 Art. 3 bis: the special DO 'Secano Interior' is for País and Cinsault from listed dry-farmed areas such as Cauquenes, Chillán, Coelemu and Yumbel.

Wines of Chile: Limarí is recognized for calcareous soils and Chardonnay; its morning fog is called 'la camanchaca'; Casablanca is Chile's pioneering cool-climate region; Colchagua has the largest Carménère plantings; Maule has old dry-farmed, head-trained vines and Carignan.

INV report: Law 25.163 sets three tiers: Indicación de Procedencia (IP) for table and regional wines, needing at least 80 percent from the named area; Indicación Geográfica (IG) for quality wines; Denominación de Origen Controlada (DOC), the strictest.

INV report (2022 data): Argentina has 110 IGs and 2 DOCs; the most used IGs in 2022 were Valle de Uco (41 percent), Patagonia (13), Valles del Famatina (8), Valles Calchaquíes (7) and Mendoza (7); the most used DOC was Luján de Cuyo.

INV list: the DOCs are Luján de Cuyo (Resolution C.15/2005) and San Rafael (C.31/2007), both in Mendoza; Cuyo IG covers Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis; Patagonia IG is interjurisdictional; Valle de Uco IG covers the San Carlos, Tunuyán and Tupungato departments; Paraje Altamira IG is in San Carlos.

INV list: IGs outside Cuyo and Patagonia include Valle de Cafayate and Cachi (Salta), Belén (Catamarca), Famatina and Chilecito (La Rioja), Colonia Caroya (Córdoba), and Balcarce and Chapadmalal (Buenos Aires); only 'Valle de Cafayate' may be used because Cafayate is a registered trademark.

Montevideo Portal, citing the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura's 2020 harvest statistics: of Uruguay's 5,991 ha of vineyard, 1,610 ha are Tannat, grown mainly in Canelones in the south; Tannat's cradle is the Madiran appellation and Uruguay was the first country to cultivate it [outside France].

Wine Australia GI register: the South Eastern Australia zone incorporates the whole of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania and only part of Queensland and South Australia; the Hunter Valley zone holds the Hunter region with subregions Broke Fordwich, Pokolbin and Upper Hunter Valley; Great Southern's subregions are Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker and Porongurup; Eden Valley's subregion is High Eden; Adelaide Hills' subregions are Lenswood and Piccadilly Valley.

Wine Australia blending rules: single vintage, variety and GI claims need at least 85 percent; up to three GIs may be claimed, each over 5 percent, listed in descending order; 83% Barossa Valley + 13% Heathcote + 4% Pemberton may be labeled 'Barossa Valley Heathcote' but not Pemberton.
Wine Australia: fruit harvested after 1 September and on or before 31 December takes the following calendar year as its vintage.
Wine Australia: descriptors such as 'Barossa style' or 'Champagne method' are not permitted, even when the true origin is shown.

Wine Australia: the Label Integrity Program (Part VIA, Wine Australia Act 2013) requires everyone in the supply chain to keep records backing vintage, variety and GI claims, made within three days of supply, receipt or processing.
New Zealand Winegrowers: regions extend 1,600 km from Northland to Central Otago; no vineyard is more than 130 km from the ocean; most regions are on the eastern coasts in the mountains' rain shadow.

New Zealand Winegrowers: Marlborough has almost 31,000 ha of vines, around two-thirds of the national total; its subregions are the Wairau Valley, the Southern Valleys and the Awatere Valley (cooler, drier, windier).
New Zealand Winegrowers: Hawke's Bay is the second largest region; vines were first planted in 1851 by Marist missionaries; the plains include the Gimblett Gravels and Bridge Pa Triangle.

New Zealand Winegrowers: Central Otago subregions are Gibbston (highest, ripens later), Bannockburn (warm, dry; harvest up to a month ahead), Cromwell/Lowburn/Pisa, Bendigo, Wanaka and Alexandra (most southerly).
New Zealand Winegrowers: Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand launched in 1995 and certifies 98 percent of vineyard area; 10 percent of wineries hold organic certification.
WOSA: origin control was enforced by law in 1973; 'Wine of Origin' with a production area means 100 percent of the grapes come from that area.

WOSA: units run geographical unit, region, district, ward, unit for estate wine, and single vineyard (no more than 6 hectares); six geographical units are Western Cape, Northern Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Free State; geographical units were provided for on 2 April 1993.

WOSA: Cape Coastal is an overarching region including the Cape South Coast and the Coastal Region, for blending maritime wines; the Cederberg and Bamboes Bay wards are not part of a district; estate wine is grown, produced and bottled on that unit.

WOSA: the Western Cape has five regions: Breede River Valley, Cape South Coast, Coastal Region, Klein Karoo and Olifants River; there are 32 districts and some 102 wards; around 86,525 ha of wine grapes over some 800 km.

WOSA: Constantia, in the Cape Town district, is the cradle of Cape winemaking, origin of Constantia dessert wines famous in 18th-century Europe; the Northern Cape's Orange River area stretches along 350 km of river; Sutherland, South Africa's coldest town, is the center of a high-altitude Northern Cape district.
Court theory guide: Areas of Study for wine law include 'Districts vs Wards in South Africa'.

unverified: Morocco: the Court lists it, but no official Moroccan source (ONSSA or similar) could be read. Secondary sources disagree on AOG/AOC counts and dates (Coteaux de l'Atlas 1998 vs 2001), so it is not taught.

Mexico's share of production from Baja California and Valle de Guadalupe differs by source (about 70%, 75% or 90%); the chapter gives no figure. Casa Madero's 1597 founding was not confirmed on the winery's own site.

Uruguay: the vineyard figures come from a news report citing the national institute's 2020 harvest statistics, not from INAVI's own pages (its site did not render). The story that Pascual Harriague brought Tannat is disputed by newer research (entry through Montevideo port), so neither version is stated.

South Africa: WOSA's Wine of Origin page lists six geographical units (Western, Northern, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Free State), matching the Court; WOSA's Winelands page lists the Western Cape plus six others including North West. The chapter uses the six on the WO page.
Australia: the blending-rules sheet suggests multiple GIs must total 95%, but the figure sits in a table whose layout did not extract cleanly; only the 'up to three GIs, each over 5%' rule is stated.

Oregon's AVA count (23) is from the Oregon Wine Board page, which may predate the newest AVAs. Washington's 22 AVAs are 'as of August 2026'; TTB established Columbia Hills on 8/17/2026 and it may not be counted.
Washington's day-night temperature swing appears as 30-40°F on one Commission page and 35-47°F on another; left out.

Argentina: the Court's 'Center Region' and 'North Region' are not IG names on the INV list; the chapter only names IGs from those provinces. The 110-IG count comes from an INV report on 2022 sales; newer IGs since then were not checked. Wines of Argentina's site is a JavaScript app and could not be read.
Chile: the Court writes 'Astral'; Decree 464 says 'Austral'. The decree PDF read on SAG's site may not include the latest amendments (e.g. Rapa Nui and Chiloé, reported in 2024).
Napa's conjunctive labeling statute was read on a public mirror (california.public.law); the official leginfo page did not render.

read.bigIdea: Every place on a U.S. label is a legal promise.
read.where: From Level 2 you know **75% grape**, **85% AVA**, **95% vintage**. At Advanced, learn where those numbers come from: **27 CFR part 4** for labels and **part 9** for AVAs. TTB lists **280** AVAs today.
read.stopsTitle: Five rules, one label at a time

stops.name: The AVA petition
stops.text: Anyone may petition. The file must prove the **name**, the **boundary** and the **distinguishing features**: climate, geology, soils, physical features and elevation.

stops.name: State, county and AVA
stops.text: A state or county needs **75%**; an AVA **85%**, and the wine must be finished in the AVA's state. Overlapping AVAs share one name at 85% from the overlap.

stops.name: Several counties or states
stops.text: Two or three counties, or two or three **contiguous** states, need **100%** of the fruit, with each share printed on the label.

stops.name: Estate bottled
stops.text: The winery is in the AVA, grows every grape on land it owns or **controls** (a lease of **3 years** or more) and keeps the wine on site from crush to bottle.

stops.name: Old names, new rules
stops.text: **Burgundy**, **Chablis**, **Champagne**, **Port** and **Sherry** are **semi-generic** in U.S. law: allowed only next to the true origin.

read.visualIntro: How much fruit each place name needs:
read.mixup: A single **county** needs **75%**. Two or three **counties** need **100%**, with each share shown.
read.sayIt: That AVA on the label means at least 85% of the grapes grew there.

read.bigIdea: The West Coast states write their own extra rules.
read.where: California makes on average **81%** of U.S. wine and holds **154** AVAs. Napa, Oregon and Washington each add something federal law does not: a **conjunctive label**, stricter **percentages**, or a soil story you must tell.

stops.name: Napa
stops.text: A wine labeled with a Napa sub-AVA such as Rutherford must also say **Napa Valley**. It applies to every wine bottled since **January 1, 1990**.

stops.name: Paso Robles
stops.text: Eleven district AVAs, including **Adelaida District** and **Templeton Gap District**, were all established on **October 9, 2014**.

stops.name: Oregon
stops.text: **90%** for a grape name (**75%** for 18 listed grapes, but not Pinot Noir), **95%** for the named place and **100%** Oregon fruit. Semi-generic names are banned. Since 2023, nested AVAs must add **Willamette Valley**.

stops.name: Washington
stops.text: Rain shadow, **6-8 inches** of rain, irrigation nearly everywhere. Wind-blown **loess** sits on **Missoula Flood** deposits over **basalt**. Five grapes make over 80% of the wine.

read.visualIntro: Federal law is the floor. Oregon builds higher:
read.mixup: Oregon's **90%** is for most grapes. **Cabernet Sauvignon** and **Syrah** sit on the **75%** list; **Pinot Noir** does not.
read.sayIt: Oregon Pinot Noir has to be at least 90% Pinot by state law.

read.bigIdea: The rest of North America: old roots, new rules.
read.where: New York nests AVAs inside AVAs: **Cayuga Lake** and **Seneca Lake** sit in the **Finger Lakes**; **North Fork** and **The Hamptons** sit in **Long Island**. The first AVA, though, was **Augusta**, Missouri.
read.stopsTitle: Four stops, east, north and south

stops.name: Other states
stops.text: **Monticello** (Virginia), **Texas High Plains** and **Texas Hill Country**, **Snake River Valley** (Idaho and Oregon), **Old Mission** and **Leelanau** peninsulas (Michigan). Missouri's state grape is **Norton**, a Vitis aestivalis.

stops.name: Ontario
stops.text: **Niagara Peninsula** has 10 sub-appellations. The region name means **85%**; a sub-appellation such as Four Mile Creek means **100%**. Icewine: picked below **-8 °C**, juice at **35° Brix**.

stops.name: B.C., Québec, Nova Scotia
stops.text: The **Okanagan Valley** has 4 sub-appellations. **Québec** leans on hybrids like **Frontenac** and **Marquette**. **Nova Scotia** is known for sparkling and the white **Tidal Bay**.

stops.name: México
stops.text: The Court calls Mexico the **oldest wine industry outside Europe**. **Valle de Guadalupe** is Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog, on sandy soils, with no appellation law.

read.visualIntro: Ontario sorts sweet wine by sugar at harvest:
read.mixup: **Augusta** (Missouri, 1980) was the **first** AVA. **Napa Valley** (1981) was the **second**.
read.sayIt: This Icewine was picked frozen on the vine, so the sweetness is all natural.

read.bigIdea: South America labels by valley, and by altitude.
read.where: Chile's **Decree 464** draws the map: six **regions**, then **subregions**, **zones** and **areas**. Argentina's **Law 25.163** sets three tiers. Uruguay's story is one grape, **Tannat**.

stops.name: Chile's map
stops.text: **Atacama**, **Coquimbo**, **Aconcagua**, **Valle Central**, **Sur** and **Austral**. A DO, grape or vintage needs **75%**. **Limarí** is known for calcareous soils and Chardonnay.

stops.name: Chile's new words
stops.text: Labels may add **Andes**, **Entre Cordilleras** or **Costa** when **85%** comes from that kind of area. **Secano Interior** is a special DO for **País** and **Cinsault** from dry-farmed land.

stops.name: Argentina
stops.text: **IP** (80%, table wine), **IG** and **DOC**. The only DOCs are **Luján de Cuyo** and **San Rafael**. **Cuyo IG** covers Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis; **Patagonia IG** spans several provinces.

stops.name: Uruguay
stops.text: In 2020, **Tannat** covered 1,610 of 5,991 ha, mostly in **Canelones**. Its cradle is **Madiran** in France.

read.visualIntro: Argentina's three tiers, strictest on top:
read.mixup: **Cuyo IG** is a whole region (Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis). **Luján de Cuyo DOC** is one small district of Mendoza.
read.sayIt: Uruguayan Tannat: dark and firm, made for grilled meat.

read.bigIdea: Down Under, the label is backed by a paper trail.
read.where: Australia's **GIs** run **zone**, **region**, **subregion**, and the **Label Integrity Program** makes everyone in the chain keep records. New Zealand's regions span **1,600 km**, none more than **130 km** from the sea.

stops.name: Australian GIs
stops.text: **South Eastern Australia** is a zone covering all of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania. Know subregions: **Pokolbin** (Hunter), **Frankland River** (Great Southern), **High Eden** (Eden Valley).

stops.name: Blending rules
stops.text: One claim needs **85%**. A blend may name up to **three GIs**, each over **5%**, in descending order. Grapes picked after **September 1** count as next year's vintage.

stops.name: Marlborough and Hawke's Bay
stops.text: **Marlborough** holds about **two-thirds** of the vines: Wairau, Southern Valleys, Awatere. **Hawke's Bay**, planted from **1851**, has the **Gimblett Gravels**.

stops.name: Central Otago
stops.text: **Gibbston** is highest and ripens later. **Bannockburn** is warm and dry and can pick a month early. **Alexandra** is most southerly.

read.mixup: **Gibbston** is the high, late-ripening subregion. **Bannockburn** is the warm, early one.
read.sayIt: Bannockburn Pinot: from one of Central Otago's warmest, driest spots.

read.bigIdea: Wine of Origin: from a whole unit to one vineyard.
read.where: From Level 2 you know the WO ladder. At Advanced, name all **six geographical units** and the Western Cape's **five regions**, and explain **districts vs wards**.

stops.name: Geographical unit
stops.text: **Western Cape**, **Northern Cape**, **Eastern Cape**, **KwaZulu-Natal**, **Limpopo** and **Free State**.

stops.name: Region
stops.text: **Breede River Valley**, **Cape South Coast**, **Coastal Region**, **Klein Karoo**, **Olifants River**. **Cape Coastal** is an overarching region for blending maritime wines.

stops.name: District
stops.text: Larger and less uniform than a ward but still with a **distinctive climate**, often drawn by mountains and rivers: **Stellenbosch**, **Paarl**, **Robertson**.

stops.name: Ward
stops.text: Small and fairly uniform, like **Constantia**. Some wards, such as **Cederberg** and **Bamboes Bay**, belong to no district.

stops.name: Estate and single vineyard
stops.text: **Estate wine** is grown, made and bottled on one unit. A **single vineyard** may not exceed **6 hectares**.

read.mixup: **Cape Coastal** is an overarching region. **Coastal Region** is one of the Western Cape's five regions inside it.
read.sayIt: Constantia: cool sea breezes, and the oldest wine story in the Cape.
